components.note: 雨 (rain) — weather, as in 雪 snow, 雷 thunder, 零 zero. Oldest form: a person waiting out rain; waiting turned into "need".
而 (ér) is only a loose sound hint here; 需 also sounds out 须 xū.
要 (want, need) — oldest form shows hands at a waist: it meant "waist" (腰 yāo adds 月 flesh); "essential" followed.

example.pinyin: Wǒ xūyào gèng duō de shíjiān.
example.fact: 需要 sits in the middle of a want/need/must spectrum: 要 alone can mean a plainer "want", 需要 is the neutral "need", and 必须 is reserved for a stronger "must" — useful for calibrating how urgent a request sounds.

examples.english: Do you need help?

examples.pinyin: Xué wàiyǔ xūyào hěn duō liànxí.
examples.english: Learning a foreign language takes a lot of practice.

components.note: 日 (sun) — on top; the usual explanation is sun over 正 "straight, correct": what is clear and straight is "right, is". A memory aid, not firm etymology.
白 (white, bright) — 的 first meant bright and clear, as in 的确 dí què.
勺 (sháo) is a loose sound clue for dì; 勺 also sounds out 约 yuē and 钓 diào.

example.fact: 是的 is a softer, more polite affirmative than a bare 是 — appending 的 turns the blunt copula "is/am" into a gentler stand-alone answer particle for confirming a question, sitting a notch more courteous than the flatter, more abrupt 对 ("correct").

examples.english: Yes, I understand.

examples.hanzi: 你是老师吗?是的,我是老师。
examples.pinyin: Nǐ shì lǎoshī ma? Shì de, wǒ shì lǎoshī.
examples.english: Are you a teacher? Yes, I am.

components.note: 歹 (bad bone) — death and decay, as in 残 remnant, 烈 fierce, 殊 special.
匕 (person) — a person beside bones: death.

example.fact: 死 is blunt, so polite speech says 去世 or 过世 for a person's death. As a degree word it means 'extremely': 累死了 'dead tired', 饿死了 'starving'. Because 四 (sì) sounds like 死 (sǐ), the number four is considered unlucky.

examples.pinyin: Zhè kē shù yǐjīng sǐ le.
examples.english: This tree has already died.
I'm dead tired today.

components.note: 欠 (open mouth, lack) — yawning, breathing and wanting: 歌 song, 欢 joy, 吹 blow; 次 also sounds out 资 zī and 瓷 cí.

example.pinyin: Wǒ qù guo liǎng cì Zhōngguó.
example.fact: 次 counts occurrences: 一次 'once', 第二次 'the second time'. Compare 遍 for a full run-through (读一遍 'read it through once'). It also means 'secondary': 次日 'the next day', 次要 'less important'.

examples.english: How many times have you been here?
This exam was hard.

components.note: 凵 (open pit) — oldest form shows a foot stepping out of a pit or cave: to go out, come out.

example.fact: 出 works as a verb and as a direction ending: 走出来 'walk out', 看出 'make out'. In compounds: 出口 'exit', 出租车 'taxi', 出发 'set off', 出生 'be born'. The opposite is 入 or 进.

examples.pinyin: Tā měitiān zǎoshang liù diǎn chūmén.
examples.english: He leaves home at six every morning.

examples.pinyin: Wǒ kàn bu chū zhè shì shénme.
examples.english: I can't tell what this is.

components.note: 阝 on the right is 邑 (city) — places, as in 都 capital, 邮 post, 部 part. 那 was a place name before it meant "that".
幺 (tiny, a thread) — 么 looks like 幺 and was borrowed as a simplified form for the light particle in 什么, 怎么, 这么. The shape does not explain the meaning today.
厶 (loop) — the visible lower part, a small curl. Memory aid: a tiny stroke 丿 over a curl — a 'little something' you ask about: 什么 what?

example.hanzi: 你想去,那么我们就一起去吧。
example.pinyin: Nǐ xiǎng qù, nàme wǒmen jiù yìqǐ qù ba.
example.english: If you want to go, then let's go together.
example.fact: 那么 mirrors 这么 (also in this batch) but points away from the speaker ("that much/so") rather than toward something close at hand — 那 vs. 这 is Mandarin's core far/near demonstrative pair, and nearly every demonstrative compound in this batch (那个/这个, 那么/这么) inherits the same contrast.

examples.english: Well then, let's begin.

examples.pinyin: Nǐ méi xiǎngdào nàme yuǎn ba?
examples.english: You didn't expect it to be that far, did you?

components.note: 干 (dry; do) — a forked pole or shield. It lends its sound to 肝 gān, 杆 gān, 赶 gǎn, 汗 hàn and 岸 àn.

example.fact: 干 gàn is the colloquial 'do': 干活 'work', 干什么 'what for?'. The same simplified character is read gān 'dry' (干净 'clean') because 乾 'dry' and 幹 'to do' were both merged into 干 in simplification.

examples.english: What do you want to do tomorrow?
He works very conscientiously.

meanings: (used before a verb or adjective for emphasis)

components.note: 阝 on the right is 邑 (city) — places, as in 都 capital, 邮 post, 部 part. 那 was a place name before it meant "that".
人 (person) — the top part. 个 is the general measure word, as in 一个, 这个, 那个.
丨 (a vertical tally) — under 人, read as one tally mark per person: counting individuals one by one.

example.fact: Beyond its literal use, 那个 (nàge) is one of Mandarin's most common hesitation fillers, like English "um" or "that thing" — and, as its own dictionary entry notes, it also serves as a euphemism for menstruation or sex in certain contexts, much as English reaches for vague stand-ins ("that time of the month") to avoid naming something directly.

examples.english: What time does that shop close?

examples.pinyin: Wǒ xiǎng yào nàge hóngsè de.
examples.english: I want that red one.

components.note: 口 (mouth) — marks speech, sounds and eating, as in 叫 call, 吃 eat, 唱 sing; 嘿 is a greeting or exclamation, hey.
黑 (hēi) — same sound: 嘿 hēi. 黑 means black.

example.fact: 嘿 grabs attention informally, like 'hey'. Doubled as 嘿嘿 it is a sly chuckle. The similar 嗨 (hāi) is a borrowed 'hi' greeting. In writing, 嘿 is rarely used in formal text.

examples.pinyin: Hēi, nǐ zài zhèr gàn shénme?
examples.english: Hey, what are you doing here?

examples.pinyin: Hēi, hǎojiǔ bú jiàn, nǐ hǎo ma?
examples.english: Hey, long time no see, how are you?

components.note: 亻 (person) — marks words about people, as in 你 you, 他 he, 做 do. Here it shows 们 pluralises person words (我们, 他们).
门 (mén) gives the sound: 们 is men (neutral tone), the same syllable as 门 gate.

example.fact: 们 makes pronouns and some nouns plural: 我们, 你们, 他们, 朋友们. It does not go with a number: 三个朋友, not 三个朋友们. Animals and objects don't take it, except in fairy-tale style.

examples.english: The children are playing in the park.

examples.hanzi: 我们明天一起去爬山吧。
examples.pinyin: Wǒmen míngtiān yìqǐ qù páshān ba.
examples.english: Let's go hiking together tomorrow.

components.note: 讠 (speech) — words and language, as in 说, 请, 谢; 话 is speech.
舌 (shé, tongue) fits the meaning (speaking) and is a loose sound clue for huà; also in 活 huó.

example.fact: 话 means 'words' or 'speech': 一句话 'a sentence', 电话 'telephone', 普通话 'Mandarin' ('common speech'). 说话 'to speak' is a verb-object phrase, so you can say 说了几句话.

examples.pinyin: Nǐ shuō de huà wǒ dōu jìde.
examples.english: I remember everything you said.

examples.pinyin: Wǒ gěi nǐ dǎ ge diànhuà ba.
examples.english: Let me give you a phone call.

components.note: 而 (and, but) — oldest form is a beard (compare 须 xū, beard), later borrowed for the conjunction; 而 survives in 耐 nài.

example.pinyin: Zhè jiā diàn piányi, érqiě hǎochī.
example.english: This restaurant is cheap, and tasty too.
example.fact: 而 is a formal connective for 'and' or 'but'. In speech it is mostly found in 而且 'moreover', 然而 'however', 因而 'therefore' and 而已 'that's all'. It is not used to join nouns the way 和 is.

examples.pinyin: Tā hěn cōngming, érqiě hěn nǔlì.
examples.english: He is smart and also hard-working.

examples.hanzi: 这个菜看起来简单，而做起来很难。
examples.pinyin: Zhège cài kàn qǐlái jiǎndān, ér zuò qǐlái hěn nán.
examples.english: This dish looks simple, yet it's hard to make.

meanings: suffix in 什么, 怎么, 这么

components.note: 幺 (tiny, a thread) — 么 looks like 幺 and was borrowed as a simplified form for the light particle in 什么, 怎么, 这么. The shape does not explain the meaning today.
厶 (loop) — the visible lower part, a small curl. Memory aid: a tiny stroke 丿 over a curl — a 'little something' you ask about: 什么 what?

example.fact: 么 appears almost only in a few common words: 什么 'what', 怎么 'how', 这么 'so', 那么 'such', 多么 'how (much)'. Don't confuse 么 with 幺 (yāo), the 'one' read in phone numbers.

examples.english: What are you saying?
How are we getting to the airport?

components.note: 东 (east) — simplified from 東; a common memory aid is the sun 日 caught in a tree 木 at sunrise.
西 (west) — traditionally a bird settling on its nest at sunset, hence west; 西 turns up in 要 and 栖.

example.pinyin: Wǒ yào qù shāngdiàn mǎi dōngxi.
example.english: I'm going to the store to buy things.
example.fact: A popular (though linguistically disputed) folk etymology traces 东西 ("thing") back to old market culture, where goods were sold from stalls clustered along a street's east and west sides — so "going to buy east-west" came to mean "going to buy things". Note the tone shift: dōngxī (both syllables toned) is the literal "east and west", while dōngxi (neutral second syllable) is the everyday noun "thing".

examples.pinyin: Wǒ de dōngxi dōu zài bāo lǐ.
examples.english: All my things are in the bag.
What's on the table?

components.note: 广 (building, shelter) — the roof-and-wall frame, as in 店, 床, 度. Here it is mostly the outline of the old 應.
心 (heart) — hidden in the traditional 應, 'respond from the heart'; simplification dropped it. 应 is yīng (should) or yìng (respond).
讠 (speech) — words, as in 说, 请, 谢: 该 is what one ought to say or do.
亥 (hài) is a close sound clue for gāi; 亥 also sounds out 孩 hái, 核 hé and 刻 kè.

example.fact: 该 alone already means "should, ought to" (as in 该不该, "should or shouldn't"), while 应 separately contributes a sense of "corresponding to what's fitting" — 应该 reinforces two near-synonymous halves into one word, the same word-building strategy seen in 喜欢 (also in this batch).

examples.english: You shouldn't be late.

examples.hanzi: 这么晚了,他应该到家了。
examples.pinyin: Zhème wǎn le, tā yīnggāi dào jiā le.
examples.english: It's so late; he should be home by now.

components.note: 子 (child) — children and offspring, as in 孙 grandchild, 学 study, 字 character; 孩 is a young child.
亥 (hài) is a close sound clue for hái; 亥 also sounds out 该 gāi, 核 hé and 刻 kè.
子 (child) — a picture of a baby with arms outstretched and legs bundled. As a suffix (孩子, 房子) it is a light noun ending.

example.pinyin: Zhè duì fūqī yǒu liǎng gè háizi.
example.fact: 子 on its own is a pictograph of a swaddled baby (arms out, legs wrapped), and 孩 combines the "child" element 子 with the phonetic 亥 (hài) for its sound — 孩子 pairs a full meaning-bearing root with a suffix character that itself still independently means "child", a case where the suffix's shift from full word to light grammatical ending is unusually easy to see.

examples.pinyin: Wǒ jiā de háizi xǐhuan huàhuà.
examples.english: My child likes drawing.
The children are playing in the park.

components.note: 走 (walk, run) — movement, as in 赶 chase, 超 surpass, 越 cross over; 起 is to rise or get up.
己 (jǐ) is a loose sound clue for qǐ; 己 also sounds out 记 jì and 纪 jì.
来 (come) — it began as a picture of a wheat plant; the sound was borrowed for "come". 麦 (wheat) still shows it, with a root 夂 added.

example.fact: Beyond its literal sense "to get up", 起来 is one of Mandarin's most productive verb-complement suffixes: attached after almost any verb it can mean "starting to..." (哭起来, "start crying"), "up off the ground" (拿起来, "pick up"), or "in the process of assessing" (说起来, "speaking of which") — several distinct extended senses layered onto one suffix.

examples.pinyin: Tiān liàng le, tā qǐlai le.
examples.english: It got light, and he got up.
Everyone started singing.

components.note: 斤 (axe) — cutting tools, as in 新 new and 斩 chop. 所 once echoed the sound of chopping; "place" and "that which" are later borrowed uses.
人 (person) — the right-hand part. The left part is a hook-and-dot, from an old tool-like shape. Meaning 'by means of, so as to' is not shown by the parts today.
Memory aid: a person 人 using a tool to get something done — 'by means of' (可以, 所以, 以前). A mnemonic, not proven etymology.

example.hanzi: 下雨了,所以我们没去公园。
example.pinyin: Xiàyǔ le, suǒyǐ wǒmen méi qù gōngyuán.
example.english: It rained, so we didn't go to the park.
example.fact: 所以 is the fixed second half of "因为...,所以..." (also flagged at rank 15 in this batch) — where English speakers feel that using both "because" and "so" together sounds redundant, Chinese not only permits but favors keeping both halves in speech, though formal writing sometimes drops one.

examples.pinyin: Tā bìng le, suǒyǐ méi qù shàngxué.
examples.english: He was sick, so he didn't go to school.

examples.hanzi: 路很远,所以我们坐车去。
examples.pinyin: Lù hěn yuǎn, suǒyǐ wǒmen zuò chē qù.
examples.english: The road is long, so we're going by car.

components.note: 辶 (walk) — movement and place, as in 道 way, 过 pass, 近 near; the radical hints at "here / this way". The 文 part is not a useful sound clue.
此 (cǐ) is a loose sound clue for xiē; 此 also sounds out 紫 zǐ and 雌 cí. 些 is the plural-ish "some, a few".

example.pinyin: Zhèxiē shū dōu shì wǒ de.
example.fact: 些 is Mandarin's built-in marker for a small, indefinite plural ("some, a few"), so 这些 is literally "this + some" — swapping in 那 or 哪 gives 那些 ("those") and 哪些 ("which ones"), the same plural-marking job that 们 does for personal pronouns, just for demonstratives instead.

examples.english: How much are these apples?
I like these photos.

components.note: 才 (talent, just) — a sprout pushing out of the ground. 才 also sounds out 材 cái and 财 cái.

example.english: He doesn't get up until eight.
example.fact: 才 stresses that something is late or hard: 八点才起床 'only at eight'. Compare 就: 八点就起床 'already at eight'. The same sound gives 人才 'talented person' and 才能 'ability', which keep the older meaning.

examples.english: Why are you only getting here now?

examples.pinyin: Wǒ zuótiān shí'èr diǎn cái shuìjiào.
examples.english: I didn't go to bed until twelve yesterday.

components.note: 两 (liǎng) — two, a pair; as a part it sounds out 辆 liàng and 俩 liǎ.

example.fact: 两 is 'two' before a measure word (两个人), while 二 is used for counting, ordinals and numbers: 二十, 第二. 两 also means a small number: 过两天 'in a couple of days'. It is the old unit 'tael' in weights too.

examples.pinyin: Qǐng gěi wǒ liǎng zhāng diànyǐngpiào.
examples.english: Please give me two movie tickets.

examples.pinyin: Wǒmen liǎng ge rén yìqǐ chīfàn.
examples.english: The two of us are having a meal together.

components.note: 钅 (metal, simplified 金) — metals, as in 钱 money, 铁 iron, 铜 copper; 错 first meant to inlay metal.
昔 (xī) is a loose sound clue for cuò; 昔 also sounds out 借 jiè, 措 cuò and 惜 xī.

example.fact: 错 is 'wrong': 你错了, 没错 'right!'. It also forms 不错 'not bad', a common mild praise. Its original sense 'to inlay metal' survives in the old term 错金 'gold inlay'.

examples.pinyin: Nǐ xiěcuò le yí ge zì.
examples.english: You wrote one character wrong.

examples.pinyin: Zhè shì wǒ de cuò, duìbuqǐ.
examples.english: It's my mistake, I'm sorry.

components.note: 辶 (walk) — movement, as in 过, 近, 送: 还 is to go back or return (huán), then "still" (hái).
不 here stands in for 睘 (huán) in the traditional 還, so it is not a real clue; same stand-in in 环 huán.
月 (flesh/meat, not moon here) — oldest form is a hand holding a piece of meat, "to possess"; 月 as meat also appears in 肉 words like 肚 belly and 脑 brain.

example.english: There's still some fruit in the fridge.
example.fact: 还 carries a core sense of "still, yet" that recurs across a whole family of common words (还是 "still/or", 还没 "not yet") — 还有 simply attaches that "still" sense to 有 ("to have") to get "there still is/remains", and spotting 还's recurring meaning helps a learner parse the whole family at once.

examples.pinyin: Nǐ hái yǒu bié de wèntí ma?
examples.english: Do you have any other questions?

examples.pinyin: Zhuōzi shàng hái yǒu liǎng běn shū.
examples.english: There are still two books on the table.

components.note: 又 (right hand) — a picture of a hand, now used for again, as in 又来了. Same hand appears inside 友 friend, 取 take, 双 pair.

example.fact: 又 is for repeats that have already happened (他又来了) and for 'both…and…': 又大又好 'both big and good'. For repeats still to come, use 再. 又 is a hand shape, which is why it appears in other hand-related characters.

examples.english: It's raining again today.
He is both smart and hard-working.

components.note: 小 (small) — three small dots, tiny grains. As a radical it appears in 少 few, 尖 sharp.

example.pinyin: Wǒ yǒu yì zhī xiǎo māo.
example.fact: 小 prefixes names for familiarity: 小王 'young Wang'. It also means 'humble' in 小店 'my humble shop'. The opposite is 大, and 小心 'be careful' literally means 'small heart'.

examples.english: This room is too small.
The kids are singing.

components.note: 中 (middle) — a line through the middle of a box, a centre mark. 中 gives sound to 钟 zhōng, 种 zhǒng, 忠 zhōng and 衷 zhōng.

example.fact: 中 is 'middle', as in 中国 'China' (the 'central country'). It is read zhòng when it means 'to hit': 中奖 'win a prize', 中毒 'be poisoned'. Be careful: 中 zhōng and 钟 zhōng sound alike.

examples.english: They're sitting in the middle.
Do you want to learn Chinese?

components.note: 口 (mouth) — calling and speech: 吗, 喊, 呼; 叫 is to shout.
丩 (jiū) is a loose clue; it also sounds out 纠 jiū.

example.fact: 叫 gives names: 我叫… 'I'm called…'. It means 'to call out' (叫他来 'tell him to come'), and in speech marks a passive: 我叫他骗了. 叫 plus a person is common for ordering a taxi: 叫出租车.

examples.english: What is her name?

examples.pinyin: Qǐng nǐ jiào yí liàng chūzūchē.
examples.english: Please call a taxi.

components.note: 口 (mouth) — marks speech, sounds and eating, as in 叫 call, 吃 eat, 唱 sing; 嗯 is a sound of agreement or acknowledgement.
恩 (ēn) — same sound: 嗯 ēn.

example.fact: 嗯 is a backchannel sound whose tone sets the meaning: a falling tone agrees ('yes'), a rising tone asks 'what?', and a flat sound expresses thinking. Mainland dictionaries mark these as ń, ň, ǹ.

examples.english: Hmm, that's a good idea.

examples.pinyin: Ēn, hǎo de, wǒ mǎshàng lái.
examples.english: Mm-hm, OK, I'll be right there.

components.note: 讠 (speech) — words, as in 说, 请, 谢: 该 is what one ought to say or do.
亥 (hài) is a close sound clue for gāi; 亥 also sounds out 孩 hái, 核 hé and 刻 kè.

example.fact: 该 means 'should' or 'it's time': 该吃饭了 'time to eat'. It can mean 'it's your turn' (该你了) and, strongly, 'must be' (这该是他的 'this must be his'). The full word 应该 is also very common.

examples.english: It's time to eat now.

examples.pinyin: Nǐ bù gāi zhème wǎn cái shuì.
examples.english: You shouldn't go to bed this late.

components.note: ⺮ (bamboo) — bamboo slips arranged in an even row; 等 means "rank, equal" and then "wait".
寺 (sì) is only a loose sound clue for děng; 寺 also in 诗 shī and 持 chí.

example.fact: 等 is 'wait': 等我 'wait for me'. Doubled 等等 as a list ender means 'etc.', and 等 can mean 'class/grade' (一等奖 'first prize'). The word 平等 'equality' keeps the older sense of 'equal'.

examples.english: Wait for me a moment.
We'll wait for you at the door.

components.note: 门 (mén, gate) is a close sound clue for wèn; the picture is asking at a gate, as in 闻 wén.
口 (mouth) — speaking, as in 吃, 唱, 叫: asking is a mouth action.
页 (head, page) — heads and faces, as in 头 head, 顶 top, 额 forehead; 题 first meant forehead, then "heading".
是 (shì) gives a loose sound clue for tí; 是 also sounds out 提 tí and 堤 dī.

example.pinyin: Wǒ yǒu yí gè wèntí xiǎng wèn nǐ.
example.english: I have a question I want to ask you.
example.fact: 问题 covers both a neutral "question" and a negative "problem" in one word, where English usually splits the two — which is why 没问题 (literally "no question") is the standard, extremely common way to say "no problem, that's fine", best learned as a fixed phrase rather than translated piece by piece.

examples.english: This question is hard to answer.

examples.pinyin: Méi wèntí, wǒ lái bāng nǐ.
examples.english: No problem, I'll help you.

components.note: 一 (one) — a single horizontal stroke is the number one; 二 and 三 just add strokes, so the first three numbers are tally marks.
走 (walk, run) — movement, as in 赶 chase, 超 surpass, 越 cross over; 起 is to rise or get up.
己 (jǐ) is a loose sound clue for qǐ; 己 also sounds out 记 jì and 纪 jì.

example.fact: 起 carries a core sense of "to rise, to arise" (as in 起来, also in this batch, and 起床 "to get out of bed") — 一起 literally combines "one" with "rise", an old image of several things "rising as one" that gave the word its modern sense, "together".

examples.english: Let's go eat together.
He lives together with his friends.

components.note: 手 (hand) — the bottom form shows a hand; 拿 is two hands closing 合 on something: to take hold.

example.pinyin: Nǐ kěyǐ ná wǒ de shū.
example.fact: 拿 is 'take in hand', unlike 带 (take along). It forms 拿手 'good at' and 拿出来 'take out'. In 把 sentences it often appears: 把书拿来 'bring the book'.

examples.pinyin: Wǒ qù ná yíxià wǒ de bāo.
examples.english: I'm going to get my bag.

examples.pinyin: Nǐ názhe zhège, wǒ qù kāimén.
examples.english: Hold this, I'll go open the door.

components.note: 曰 (say) — the middle part, a mouth-like box. 更 is a sound-borrowed shape today; the visible parts do not explain 'more / change'. Memory aid: one (一) more thing to say.

example.english: Today is even colder than yesterday.
example.fact: 更 (gèng) means 'even more' in comparisons: 更好 'even better'. It is read gēng when it means 'to change' (更新 'update') or an old watch of the night (三更半夜 'in the dead of night').

examples.english: This one is even better than that one.

examples.pinyin: Wǎnshang de fēng gèng dà le.
examples.english: The wind got even stronger at night.

components.note: 廾 (two hands) — in 開 two hands lift the bar of a gate; 开 is the simplified shape. Compare 关 (close).
女 (woman) — women and family, as in 妈 mom, 好 good, 姐 sister.
台 (tái) is a loose sound clue for shǐ; the same 台 gives 治 zhì and 怡 yí.

example.english: What time does the movie start?
example.fact: 开 pictures two hands (廾) lifting away a door's latch (一) — the act of "opening" something shut — while 始 is traditionally linked to 女 ("woman") as a source of origin. 开始 pairs "to open" with "to originate" into a vivid literal image of throwing open a beginning.

examples.english: It's snowing, and the match has begun.
I started learning to swim yesterday.

components.note: 巾 (cloth) — cloth, as in 布, 带, 帽: 帮 first meant the side of a shoe.
邦 (bāng, nation) gives the exact sound; 邦 itself means state or country.

example.english: Let me help you carry it.
example.fact: 帮 takes a person and a verb: 帮我开门 'help me open the door'. 帮忙 'to help out' is verb-object: 帮个忙 'do me a favour'. The formal word is 帮助. Simplified from 幫.

examples.hanzi: 你能帮我拿一下行李吗？
examples.pinyin: Nǐ néng bāng wǒ ná yíxià xíngli ma?
examples.english: Can you help me carry the luggage?

examples.hanzi: 谢谢你帮我找到了手机。
examples.pinyin: Xièxie nǐ bāng wǒ zhǎodàole shǒujī.
examples.english: Thank you for helping me find my phone.

components.note: 扌 (hand) — hand actions, as in 拿, 抱, 把; 打 is to hit.
丁 (dīng) is a loose sound clue for dǎ; 丁 also sounds out 订 dìng, 顶 dǐng and 钉 dīng.

example.fact: 打 is far more than 'hit': 打电话 'make a phone call', 打车 'take a taxi', 打伞 'hold an umbrella', 打折 'give a discount'. It is the verb of choice for many hand actions and ball sports.

examples.english: Please call me.

examples.hanzi: 我们周末去打乒乓球吧。
examples.pinyin: Wǒmen zhōumò qù dǎ pīngpāngqiú ba.
examples.english: Let's go play table tennis this weekend.

components.note: 友 (friend) replaces the heart-and-foot lower part of the traditional 愛, which had 心 (heart); so 爱 lost its heart in simplification.

example.fact: 爱 as 'love' is stronger than English in couples' talk: 我爱你 is used less casually than 'I love you'. As a habit verb it means 'fond of': 他爱吃辣 'He loves spicy food'. The simplified form drops the 心 of 愛, a fact Chinese learners often joke about.

examples.pinyin: Wǒ ài tīng lǎoshī jiǎng gùshi.
examples.english: I love listening to the teacher tell stories.
Kids all love eating candy.

components.note: 巾 (cloth) — cloth, as in 布, 帽, 帮: a belt of cloth with pieces hanging from it.

example.english: I take my child to the park.
example.fact: 带 means 'carry along' or 'lead': 带路 'show the way', 带孩子 'look after a child'. It differs from 拿 'hold in hand'. As a noun it means 'belt' or 'zone': 一带 'the area'.

examples.english: Don't forget to bring your keys when you go out.
Did you bring an umbrella?

components.note: 日 (sun) — day and time, as in 晴 clear, 早 early, 明 bright; time was read from the sun.
寸 (cùn) stands in for 寺 sì in the traditional 時; sound clue is loose. 寺 also gives 诗 shī and 持 chí.
门 (gate) — doors and openings, as in 问 ask, 开 open, 关 close.
日 (sun) — a gap in the gate lets daylight through (the traditional 間 had 月 moon): the space between.

example.fact: 时间 names time as a general concept or duration (没有时间 "no time"), while its near-synonym 时候 (also in this batch, rank 19) marks one specific moment and almost always sits inside a "...的时候" clause. 间 itself contributes a spatial sense of "a space between" — literally, 时间 frames time as the gap between moments.

examples.english: Do you have time?

examples.hanzi: 这件事花了我很多时间。
examples.pinyin: Zhè jiàn shì huāle wǒ hěn duō shíjiān.
examples.english: This took me a lot of time.

components.note: 年 (year) — first drawn as a person carrying harvested grain: one harvest per year. Seen in 今年, 去年, 年轻.

example.fact: 年 counts years: 三年, 去年 'last year', 明年 'next year'. 过年 means 'celebrate the Lunar New Year'. In its oldest sense it referred to the grain harvest. 年 is a measure of time only: use 岁 for age.

examples.english: I'm twenty-five this year.

examples.pinyin: Wǒ zài zhèlǐ zhùle sān nián.
examples.english: I've lived here for three years.

components.note: 讠 (speech, simplified 言) — talking and asking: 说, 谢, 谈; 请 is to ask politely.
青 (qīng) sounds like 请 (tone differs); same part in 清, 情, 晴, 精, 静.

example.fact: 请 + verb is the polite 'please': 请进 'please come in', 请问 'excuse me, may I ask'. 请客 means 'to treat someone', and 请假 'ask for leave'. It is also 'to hire': 请老师 'engage a teacher'.

examples.english: Excuse me, where is the restroom?

examples.pinyin: Wǒ xiǎng qǐng nǐ chī wǎnfàn.
examples.english: I'd like to treat you to dinner.

components.note: 回 (return) — a swirl or whirlpool drawn as nested squares: it turns around and comes back.

example.fact: 回 is the word for going back to where you came from: 回家, 回国, 回来. It is also a measure word for occurrences in speech (去过两回 'been twice'), and it appears in 回答 'to answer' and 回忆 'to recall'.

examples.english: When are you going back to your country?

examples.pinyin: Qǐng nǐ huídá wǒ de wèntí.
examples.english: Please answer my question.

components.note: 工 (work) — a carpenter's tool shape: work, craftsman. 工 is a sound series: 红 hóng, 江 jiāng, 功 gōng, 空 kōng.
亻 (person) — people, as in 你, 他, 做: 作 is something a person does or makes.
乍 (zuò) gives the exact sound; 乍 also in 昨 zuó, 炸 zhà and 怎 zěn.

example.pinyin: Tā měitiān gōngzuò bā gè xiǎoshí.
example.english: He works eight hours every day.
example.fact: 工作 functions as both a verb ("to work") and a noun ("job, work") with no change in form at all — a common feature of Chinese words that switch grammatical role for free, where English sometimes needs an entirely different word ("to work" vs. "a job").

examples.english: She works at a bank.
Have you found a job?

components.note: 灬 (fire) — heat and burning, as in 热 hot, 点 dot, 照 shine. 然 first meant "to burn" (燃 rán adds 火 later); "so, naturally" is borrowed.
肰 (rán) gives the exact sound and shows up in 燃 rán.
后 (after, behind) — two words merged in simplified writing: old 后 "ruler" (皇后 empress) and 後 "behind, later" (as in 然后).

example.hanzi: 我们先吃饭,然后去看电影。
example.pinyin: Wǒmen xiān chīfàn, ránhòu qù kàn diànyǐng.
example.english: We'll eat first, then go watch a movie.
example.fact: 然后 is the standard connector for sequencing actions, often paired with 先 ("first") as here — but in casual storytelling it's also notorious as a near-meaningless filler that Mandarin speakers chain sentence after sentence ("...然后...然后..."), much like English speakers lean on "so" or "and then" when narrating.

examples.english: Wash your hands first, then eat.

examples.pinyin: Tā shuōwán ránhòu jiù zǒu le.
examples.english: After he finished speaking, he left.

components.note: 當 (traditional) — 田 field under 尚 (shàng), 尚 being a loose sound hint for dāng. 当 keeps only a squashed top and a few strokes of it.
尚 (shàng) — the top part of 當; only a loose sound clue today. 当 is dāng (to act as, should) or dàng (appropriate).

example.pinyin: Wǒ zhǎngdà le xiǎng dāng lǎoshī.
example.english: When I grow up I want to be a teacher.
example.fact: 当 means 'to act as': 当老师 'be a teacher', and in 当时 'at that time' it marks a moment. Read as dàng it is 'to treat as': 当真 'take seriously', 上当 'be fooled'. The two readings change the meaning.

examples.hanzi: 当我到家的时候，天已经黑了。
examples.pinyin: Dāng wǒ dào jiā de shíhou, tiān yǐjīng hēi le.
examples.english: When I got home, it was already dark.
He has been a teacher for ten years.

components.note: 见 (see) — a big eye on a person's legs 儿: a person looking. The same 见 is in 现 appear, 觉 sense, 视 look.

example.fact: 见 often follows other verbs as a result: 看见 'catch sight of', 听见 'hear'. 见面 'meet in person' is a verb-object word, so you say 见了面. 再见 'goodbye' literally means 'see again'.

examples.english: I met an old friend yesterday.

examples.pinyin: Nǐ kànjiàn wǒ de yàoshi le ma?
examples.english: Have you seen my keys?

components.note: 钅 (metal) — 钅 is the simplified 金 (metal), as in 铁, 银, 钟; early money was metal coins.
戋 (jiān) — near sound — 钱 is qián; 戋 also sounds out 浅 qiǎn and 线 xiàn, and means small or thin.

example.fact: 钱 is 'money': 多少钱 'how much', 零钱 'small change', 没钱 'broke'. Chinese counts it with 块 (kuài) in speech: 五块钱. 钱 is also a common surname, pronounced the same.

examples.english: I didn't bring any money with me.

examples.pinyin: Zhè jiàn yīfu yào sānbǎi kuài qián.
examples.english: This dress costs three hundred yuan.

components.note: 一 (one) — a single horizontal stroke is the number one; 二 and 三 just add strokes, so the first three numbers are tally marks.
木 (tree) — wood, as in 桌 table, 板 board; 样 once meant a tree (acorn) and later "form, pattern".
羊 (yáng, sheep) is a near-exact sound clue for yàng; 羊 also sounds out 洋 yáng and 养 yǎng.

example.hanzi: 这两个杯子看起来一样。
example.pinyin: Zhè liǎng gè bēizi kàn qǐlai yíyàng.
example.english: These two cups look the same.
example.fact: 一样 does its real work inside the comparison frame "A 跟/和 B 一样(+adjective)" ("A is the same as B", e.g. 我跟你一样高, "I'm as tall as you") — one of the core building blocks of Chinese comparison sentences, alongside 比 ("more than"), beyond its plain gloss of "same".

examples.english: I'm as tall as you.
Their ideas are not the same.

components.note: 彐 (hand-like part) — 事 is usually explained as a hand holding a tool or tally, 'handling business' — a hedged reading, not certain.
史 (history, scribe) — shares an ancient root with 事: a hand holding a recording tool. Both are about handling official 'matters'.
忄 (heart) — feelings, as in 快 happy, 怕 afraid, 忙 busy.
青 (qīng) is a close sound clue for qíng; the series 清 qīng, 请 qǐng, 晴 qíng, 精 jīng.

example.hanzi: 我今天有很多事情要做。
example.pinyin: Wǒ jīntiān yǒu hěn duō shìqing yào zuò.
example.english: I have a lot of things to do today.
example.fact: 事情 covers abstract matters, affairs, and tasks — never a physical object. For a physical "thing" Chinese instead reaches for 东西 (also in this batch, rank 32); English "thing" blurs both senses into one word, but Chinese keeps the abstract/concrete split strict between these two very common nouns.

examples.pinyin: Zhè shì yí jiàn yǒuqù de shìqing.
examples.english: This is an interesting matter.

examples.hanzi: 他们忙着处理工作上的事情。
examples.pinyin: Tāmen mángzhe chǔlǐ gōngzuò shàng de shìqing.
examples.english: They're busy handling work matters.
